{{short description|Theorem stating that smooth algebraic curve has minimum genus its homology class}}
In [[mathematics]], a smooth [[algebraic curve]] <math>C</math> in the [[complex projective plane]], of degree <math>d</math>, has [[Genus_(mathematics)#Topology|genus]] given by the [[genus–degree formula]] 

:<math>g = (d-1)(d-2)/2</math>.

The '''Thom conjecture''', named after French mathematician [[René Thom]], states that if <math>\Sigma</math> is any smoothly embedded connected curve representing the same class in [[homology (mathematics)|homology]] as <math>C</math>, then the genus <math>g</math> of <math>\Sigma</math> satisfies the inequality

:<math>g \geq (d-1)(d-2)/2</math>.

In particular, ''C'' is known as a ''genus minimizing representative'' of its homology class. It was first proved by [[Peter B. Kronheimer|Peter Kronheimer]] and [[Tomasz Mrowka]] in October 1994,<ref>{{Cite journal|title = The Genus of Embedded Surfaces in the Projective Plane|journal = Mathematical Research Letters|volume = 1|issue = 6|pages= 797–808|doi = 10.4310/mrl.1994.v1.n6.a14| first1 = Peter B.|last1 = Kronheimer|authorlink1=Peter B. Kronheimer|first2 = Tomasz S.|last2 = Mrowka|authorlink2=Tomasz Mrowka|year = 1994|doi-access = free}}</ref> using the then-new [[Seiberg–Witten invariant]]s.  

Assuming that <math>\Sigma</math> has nonnegative self [[intersection number]] this was generalized to [[Kähler manifold]]s (an example being the complex projective plane) by [[John Morgan (mathematician)|John Morgan]], [[Zoltán Szabó (mathematician)|Zoltán Szabó]], and [[Clifford Taubes]],<ref>{{cite journal | first1=John | last1=Morgan| authorlink1=John Morgan (mathematician)|
last2=Szabó | first2=Zoltán | authorlink2=Zoltán Szabó (mathematician) |
first3=Clifford| last3=Taubes| authorlink3=Clifford Taubes| title=A product formula for the Seiberg-Witten invariants and the generalized Thom conjecture| 
journal=[[Journal of Differential Geometry]]| volume= 44 |year=1996|issue= 4|pages= 706–788|mr=1438191|doi=10.4310/jdg/1214459408| doi-access=free}}</ref>  also using the Seiberg–Witten invariants.  

There is at least one generalization of this conjecture, known as the [[Symplectic geometry|symplectic]] Thom conjecture (which is now a theorem, as proved for example by [[Peter Ozsváth]] and Szabó in 2000<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ozsváth |first1=Peter|authorlink1=Peter Ozsváth |last2=Szabó |first2=Zoltán |authorlink2=Zoltán Szabó (mathematician) | year=2000 |title=The symplectic Thom conjecture |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |volume=151 |issue=1 |pages=93–124 |arxiv=math.DG/9811087 |doi=10.2307/121113|jstor=121113|s2cid=5283657 }}</ref>). It states that a symplectic surface of a symplectic 4-manifold is genus minimizing within its homology class. This would imply the previous result because algebraic curves (complex dimension 1, real dimension 2) are symplectic surfaces within the complex projective plane, which is a symplectic 4-manifold.
